content.content:
## Giving Credit Where Credit Is Due

Whenever you use someone else's ideas, words, data, or arguments in your academic writing, you must give them proper credit. This is not just a matter of politeness -- it is a fundamental principle of academic integrity. Failing to cite your sources is considered **plagiarism**, which can result in serious academic consequences.

Citation serves several important purposes: it acknowledges the original author's intellectual contribution, allows readers to locate and verify your sources, strengthens your argument by showing it is grounded in existing research, demonstrates the breadth of your research, and protects you from accusations of plagiarism. In this chapter you will learn why citation is essential, how to format in-text citations in both APA and MLA styles, how to create reference list entries, and how to recognize and avoid different forms of plagiarism. The golden rule throughout is simple: when in doubt, cite.

## APA versus MLA

The two most widely used citation styles in English-language academia are **APA** (American Psychological Association) and **MLA** (Modern Language Association). **APA style** (7th edition) is used primarily in the social sciences, psychology, education, and business. Its in-text format is **(Author, Year)** -- for example, (Smith, 2023) -- with a page number added for direct quotes: (Smith, 2023, p. 45). Its reference list is titled **References**. **MLA style** (9th edition) is used primarily in the humanities, literature, languages, and arts. Its in-text format is **(Author Page)** -- for example, (Smith 45) -- with no comma between author and page number. Its reference list is titled **Works Cited**.

The key differences are easy to remember: APA includes the year in the citation and emphasizes the date of publication, while MLA omits the year and emphasizes the author's name. To see them side by side, a paraphrase from a 2021 book by Sarah Johnson would be cited as "(Johnson, 2021)" in APA but "(Johnson 42)" in MLA. A direct quote from page 87 would be "Johnson (2021)... (p. 87)" in APA but "Johnson... (87)" in MLA. For two authors, APA uses an ampersand -- (Brown & Chen, 2019) -- while MLA uses "and": (Brown and Chen 112). For three or more authors, both styles use "et al." from the first citation. In both styles, the period goes *after* the parenthetical citation, and signal phrases ("Johnson states that...") integrate citations more naturally into your prose. Which to use? Follow your teacher's or institution's guidelines -- in Norway, APA is more common in secondary schools and universities, though both are widely accepted.

questions.task: What is the in-text citation format in APA style?
questions.solution: APA uses (Author, Year), such as (Smith, 2023), with a page number added for direct quotes. MLA uses (Author Page), such as (Smith 45).

questions.task: How does MLA differ from APA in its in-text citation?

options.text: MLA uses (Author Page) and omits the year

questions.solution: MLA uses (Author Page) -- such as (Smith 45) -- omitting the year and emphasizing the author's name, while APA includes the year and emphasizes the publication date.

questions.task: For three or more authors, what do both APA and MLA use?

options.text: All authors' full names every time

questions.solution: Both APA and MLA use 'et al.' for three or more authors (e.g., Williams et al.) from the first citation onward.

questions.task: Which citation style is more common in Norwegian secondary schools and universities?
questions.solution: In Norway, APA is more commonly used in secondary schools and universities, though both APA and MLA are widely accepted. Always follow your institution's guidelines.

content.content:
## Plagiarism and Genuine Paraphrasing

**Plagiarism** is presenting someone else's words, ideas, or work as your own, whether intentionally or not -- and it comes in several forms. **Direct plagiarism** is copying text word-for-word without quotation marks or citation -- the most blatant form. **Mosaic plagiarism** (patchwriting) takes phrases from a source and weaves them into your own sentences without quotation marks -- common among students learning to paraphrase. **Paraphrase plagiarism** restates an author's ideas in your own words but fails to cite the source. **Self-plagiarism** is submitting your own previous work for a new assignment without permission. And **AI-generated plagiarism** is submitting text generated by AI tools as your own without disclosure -- a growing concern. To avoid all of these, always cite when you use someone else's ideas (even paraphrased), use quotation marks for borrowed phrases, paraphrase genuinely (changing both the words *and* the sentence structure), keep track of all sources, disclose AI use, and when in doubt, cite.

The difference between plagiarism and proper paraphrasing becomes clear with an example. Take this original (Smith, 2022, p. 78): "Social media algorithms create echo chambers that reinforce existing beliefs and limit exposure to diverse perspectives, thereby contributing to political polarization." Attempt 1 -- copying the sentence exactly with no quotation marks or citation -- is **direct plagiarism**. Attempt 2 -- adding a citation but keeping most of the sentence structure and key phrases, swapping only a few words ("strengthen" for "reinforce") -- is **mosaic plagiarism / patchwriting**, because genuine paraphrasing requires more than word-swapping. Attempt 3 is a **correct paraphrase**: "According to Smith (2022), the design of social media platforms tends to create insulated information environments where users primarily encounter content that aligns with their pre-existing views, a phenomenon that researchers have linked to increasing divisions in political discourse (p. 78)." Here the idea is fully restated in the writer's own words and sentence structure, with a proper citation -- the original meaning is preserved but the expression is entirely new. That is the standard to aim for.

exercise.task: Test yourself on plagiarism and paraphrasing:

options.text: Writing entirely in your own words with a citation
Quoting with quotation marks and a citation
Taking phrases from a source and weaving them into your sentences without quotation marks

questions.solution: Mosaic plagiarism (patchwriting) takes phrases from a source and weaves them into your own sentences, often swapping a few words but keeping the structure -- it is plagiarism even with a citation.

options.text: Restating the idea in entirely your own words AND sentence structure, with a citation
Swapping just a few words while keeping the structure
Copying exactly but adding a citation

questions.solution: Genuine paraphrasing means restating an idea in your own words and sentence structure, with a proper citation. Merely swapping a few words is patchwriting, a form of plagiarism.

questions.task: Which is a newer, growing form of plagiarism?

options.text: Submitting AI-generated text as your own without disclosure

questions.solution: AI-generated plagiarism -- submitting text from tools like ChatGPT as your own without disclosure -- is a growing concern in education. Disclose AI use per your school's policy.

questions.task: What is the 'golden rule' of citation?

options.text: When in doubt, cite -- it is better to over-cite than to plagiarize

questions.solution: The golden rule is: when in doubt, cite. It is always better to include a citation that may not be strictly necessary than to risk plagiarism.

## Summary

Citation is mandatory whenever you use someone else's ideas, words, or data -- whether quoting or paraphrasing -- because it upholds **academic integrity** and protects you from **plagiarism**. The two major styles differ in format: **APA** uses (Author, Year) and dominates the social sciences, while **MLA** uses (Author Page) and dominates the humanities, with a **References** or **Works Cited** page giving full details. Plagiarism takes many forms -- direct copying, mosaic plagiarism (patchwriting), paraphrase without citation, self-plagiarism, and undisclosed AI-generated content. **Genuine paraphrasing** means restating ideas in entirely your own words *and* sentence structure, with a proper citation -- not merely swapping a few words. The golden rule holds throughout: when in doubt, cite.
